cards.title: Engineer fast wins into any long-timeline offer
cards.summary: Add short-term emotional wins so clients stay committed long enough to reach the ultimate (slow) outcome they actually bought.
cards.use_when: Designing fulfillment or onboarding for an offer whose primary dream outcome takes months or years (fitness, coaching, long SaaS transformations) and you need retention and follow-through.
steps: Identify the ultimate dream outcome and the realistic time delay to achieve it (the book's example: a 'bikini body' may be 12+ months).
List ancillary benefits that can be experienced far sooner than the headline outcome: more energy, higher sex drive, social community, early visible progress.
Deliver at least one of those ancillary benefits within the first days or weeks of the client starting, even if they did not buy it explicitly.
For a fitness-style program the book describes meeting another member early for immediate social benefit and using a more aggressive initial diet to create a big, fast emotional win.

In a B2B/agency ecommerce context this maps to getting the client's ads live and a first sale closed within the first week (the book cites a $2,000 first sale in seven days) so their decision to hire you is reinforced.
Track and celebrate the fast win explicitly so the client notices it; the point is reassurance that they chose correctly, not just the win itself.
Use the momentum from the early win to get the client to adopt the rest of your system, which is what actually produces the long-term outcome.
caveats: The claim that early victories increase persistence is presented as 'backed by science' in the source but no study is cited.
A deliberately aggressive early phase can be unsuitable or risky for some clients; treat it as a situational tactic, not a universal rule.

cards.title: Competing against free: sell speed
cards.summary: When your market's alternative is free, a speed-first positioning can beat price-based competition because people pay for fast.
cards.use_when: You sell against a free or near-free alternative (organic content, free tools, DIY, government services) and cannot win on price.
steps: Identify the free alternative your prospect would otherwise use and confirm that speed is the pain point they actually feel.
Position your offer around eliminating waiting time rather than adding features the free option lacks.
Cite category precedents the book uses: paying ~$50 to skip the DMV line privately, FedEx vs USPS overnight, Spotify vs slow free music, Uber vs walking.
Make the speed claim concrete and specific (a time saved, a lead time, a turnaround window) rather than a vague 'faster' claim.
If your product can be delivered instantly (digital assets, templates, pre-built resources) lean into instant access as the differentiator.
Price against the value of the time saved, not against the free alternative's zero price.
caveats: The source asserts 'the only thing that beats free is fast'; treat as a strong opinion suited to commodity/free-dominated markets, not a universal law.
Speed positioning loses its edge once multiple competitors also compete on speed.

cards.title: Rate and improve an offer with the four value drivers
cards.summary: Score offers on dream outcome, perceived likelihood of achievement, time delay and effort/sacrifice, then engineer each in the favorable direction.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing why a comparable outcome sells for very different prices, or deciding where to strengthen an existing offer.
steps: Define the dream outcome the buyer actually wants (relaxation, weight loss, revenue) — not the vehicle you sell.
Score each of the four drivers 0 (missing) or 1 (achieved): dream outcome, perceived likelihood of achievement, time delay to achievement, effort and sacrifice.
Sum the four scores to get a rough relative value rating; use it to compare two vehicles delivering the same outcome.
Increase the dream outcome and perceived likelihood of achievement; decrease time delay and effort/sacrifice.

The book's illustrations: meditation and Xanax both deliver relaxation, but Xanax scores higher on speed and effort and is the multi-billion dollar product; supplements (~$123B, Grandview Research) outsell health clubs (~$62B, IHRSA) because pills are faster and easier than daily gym visits.
Use the diagnosis to justify pricing: the same outcome delivered through a higher-value vehicle supports a far higher price ($25,000 liposuction vs ~$100/mo bootcamp).
caveats: The 0/1 scale is a rough comparative heuristic, not a precise financial model.
Market-size figures are cited from third parties and are illustrative, not benchmarks for your business.

cards.title: Reduce effort and sacrifice to lift perceived value
cards.summary: Effort, ancillary costs and sacrifice are a value driver you can lower to make the same outcome far more appealing and pricier.
cards.use_when: Your offer requires heavy customer work, travel, learning curve or ongoing inconvenience and prospects stall or churn.
steps: List the tangible and intangible 'other costs' your buyer accrues: time in the gym, learning a system, prep work, coordination, discipline.

Compare against the competing vehicle the book uses: liposuction vs fitness carries a massive effort/sacrifice gap, which plastic surgeons exploit with copy like 'tired of wasting countless hours in the gym... tired of diets that just don't work?'

Move offerings along the DIY → done-with-you → done-for-you spectrum; the book notes done-for-you services command higher prices because the buyer carries no effort and also perceives a higher likelihood of success when an expert executes.
Reduce perceived effort with templates, guides, automation, checklists and pre-built assets rather than only adding more deliverables.

Where total removal of effort is unaffordable (e.g. moving in with a client), step back until you find a lesser version you can deliver at scale, or raise the price until the high-effort version is worth it.
State explicitly what you take off the buyer's plate in your marketing copy, since perceived effort reduction is what shifts value.
caveats: Perceived likelihood of achievement is a separate driver from effort; lowering effort alone may not overcome low credibility.
Overpromising a 'zero effort' experience you cannot operationally deliver creates refund and churn pressure.

cards.title: Use divergent thinking to invent offer variations (the brick exercise)
cards.summary: Train divergent problem-solving — many right answers to one problem — before converging on the best offer construction.
cards.use_when: You are stuck defaulting to the same offer format as competitors and need to generate many possible ways to deliver value.
steps: Recognize the contrast: convergent thinking (math-style, known variables, one right answer) is what school rewards, but the book argues business pays for divergent thinking (known and unknown variables, dynamic conditions, multiple right answers).
Run the 120-second brick exercise: set a timer and list every use of a brick you can think of.

Then vary the parameters — size (gum tab, standard 3-5/8" x 2-1/4" x 8", 2ft x 6ft), material (plastic, gold, clay, wood, metal), shape (holes, interlocking divots) — and extend the list; the book's list includes paperweight, door stop, fish home, plant holder, trophy, mural, resistance weight, flotation device, payment and store of value.
Apply the same expansion to your product: define what the customer desires, then generate as many ways as possible your 'brick' (existing asset) could create value for that desire.
Do this once per product; the book calls it high-value, high-leverage work that you only need to do a single time for an asset that may last years.
caveats: Divergent lists are intentionally unconstrained and will contain impractical ideas; convergence and trimming come later.
The exercise only helps if you follow it with customer-specific problems to solve against.

cards.title: Sell the destination, not the membership
cards.summary: Reframe what you sell as the prospect's arrived dream outcome with a compressed timeline, which resets the competitive comparison.
cards.use_when: Prospects price-compare you against a low-cost commodity (a gym membership, a generic subscription) and say you are expensive.
steps: Stop selling the vehicle ('membership', 'flight') and sell the destination ('the vacation') — the outcome as the customer would like to experience it.
Write the dream outcome with an explicit reduced time delay, as in the book's 'Lose 20lbs in 6 weeks' weight-loss challenge.
Test whether the new frame escapes direct comparison: a $99/mo bootcamp loses to a $29/mo gym membership, but a 6-week 20lb challenge is a different category.
Use the reframe as the anchor for everything else (problems, solutions, bundles, price).
caveats: A compressed-timeline promise must be deliverable; overclaiming creates refunds and reputational damage.
For ecommerce this may mean selling a transformation kit or result-based bundle rather than a product SKU; applicability depends on category.

cards.title: List every problem in sequence, using the four drivers as prompts
cards.summary: Enumerate the prospect's obstacles in order of their experience, using the four value drivers to surface 32–64 distinct problems.
cards.use_when: Building or rebuilding an offer and you need a complete obstacle inventory before designing solutions.
steps: Think in the sequence the customer experiences each obstacle; start with what happens immediately before and immediately after they use your product or service, and what their 'next' problem is.
For each core task they must do, prompt with the four drivers: Is this financially worth it? Will it work for me specifically? Will it be too hard or confusing? Will it take too much time?

The book's weight-loss example: core tasks are buying healthy food, cooking it, eating it, exercising; each carries 2–4 sub-problems (too hard, too slow, too expensive, unsustainable, family gets in the way, travel breaks it).
Write in the prospect's voice, including limiting beliefs ('I won't like it', 'I will suck at it'), not your operational language.
Expect a large list — the book counts roughly 16 core problems with 2–4 sub-problems each, 32–64 total — and treat volume as good news because every problem is a solvable value opportunity.
Do not let the four driver buckets constrain you; list anything you can think of, then organize.
caveats: More problems listed means more solutions to actually deliver; inventory must eventually be reconciled with what you can fulfill.
The four-driver prompts are a generative guide, not an exhaustive taxonomy.

cards.title: Flip each problem into a solution with 'how to' language
cards.summary: Convert the obstacle list into a solutions list by reversing each problem into solution-oriented copy.
cards.use_when: You have a problem inventory and need to define the concrete deliverables you will provide.
steps: For each problem ask: what would I need to show someone to solve this?
Reverse the obstacle into solution language; the book says simply adding 'how to' to the reversed problem is a workable starting point for newcomers.

Examples from the source: 'buying healthy food is expensive' → 'how to buy healthy food for less than your current grocery bill'; 'cooking takes too much time' → 'how to cook meals in under 5 minutes'; 'travel breaks my diet' → 'how to get healthy food when traveling'.
Expect repetition across problems — the book says that is normal because all problems relate to the same four value drivers.
Treat the solutions list as a checklist of what you must deliver, not as final marketing copy; naming and bundling come later.

Cross-check against a different category if useful: the book cites a 90-day relationship course whose problems included poor communication, no chemistry and unmet expectations, each converted into a 'how to' solution.
caveats: The source explicitly notes copywriting craft is beyond the book's scope; 'how to' reversal is a starter technique, not finished copy.
The book insists you must eventually solve every problem on the list; unresolved obstacles suppress conversion even if they are not the most common objection.

cards.title: Design delivery vehicles across personal-attention, effort and medium
cards.summary: Turn each solution into concrete delivery options by varying how many people you serve at once, how much effort the buyer exerts, and the medium.
cards.use_when: Translating a solutions list into actual deliverables you can operate and price.
steps: List options by group size: one-on-one, small group, or one-to-many.
Vary buyer effort across DIY (they figure it out), DWY (you teach them), and DFY (you do it).
Vary medium for live delivery: in-person, phone, email, text, Zoom, chat.
Vary format for recordings: audio, video or written.
Specify responsiveness: which days, which hours, and reply-time targets such as 24/7, 9–5, within 5 minutes, within an hour, within 24 hours.
Apply the 10x / 1/10th test: what would you provide if customers paid 10x your price ($100,000 in the book's framing), and how would you still make them successful at one-tenth of your price?

For a single problem like 'buying healthy food is hard', the book generates: in-person shopping together, personalized lists, full-service buying, orientation sessions, text support while shopping, live phone direction, live-streamed or recorded grocery tours, DIY calculators, pre-made weekly lists, a grocery buddy pairing, and pre-built delivery carts.
Generate options you are not willing to do — the book says this is fine and useful for stretching your thinking.
caveats: The generator produces far more than you should deliver; trimming for cost and value is a required follow-up step.
High-responsiveness promises (5-minute replies, 24/7) are expensive and should be priced or scoped accordingly.

cards.title: Trim by cost vs value, keeping low-cost/high-value first
cards.summary: Filter the delivery-vehicle list down to items that are cheap for you and valuable to the buyer, prioritizing one-to-many assets.
cards.use_when: You have a large list of possible deliverables and need to decide what actually goes into the offer.
steps: Estimate the cost to you of providing each solution.
Remove high-cost, low-value items first.
Then remove low-cost, low-value items.
Judge value against the four drivers: does it make the buyer financially better off, increase their belief they will succeed, reduce effort and sacrifice, or shorten time to result?
Keep what remains in two buckets: low cost/high value and high cost/high value; reserve the latter for big value adds only, as the book does with 1-on-1 work for portfolio CEOs scaling past $30m+.

Where a high-cost item is essential, either step back incrementally to a scalable lesser version or raise the price until the effort is worth it (the book's 'gazillion dollars to live with someone' framing).

Prioritize one-to-many assets because they typically show the largest gap between cost and value: the source's meal-plan generator took ~100 hours to build and then produced personalized plans in about 15 minutes.

Example outputs kept by the book's gym: bulking blueprints, an eating-out system, a travel eating and workout guide, meal plans by bodyweight and gender, a grocery list calculator, plateau-busting plans, fast-cooking guides, and one-on-one nutrition orientations.
caveats: One-to-many assets carry a large upfront creation cost before they pay back; the payoff assumes enough volume.
Cost and value estimates are judgments; re-evaluate as fulfillment data accumulates.

cards.title: Resolve every perceived obstacle or lose sales
cards.summary: One unaddressed objection can block a sale, so convert recurring objections into reusable assets instead of arguing the customer out of them.
cards.use_when: Prospects repeatedly raise the same 'but what about...' objection late in the sales conversation.
steps: Take the book's anecdote: the author insisted weight-loss clients prepare all food at home and lost many sales to objections about eating out; a business exec about to walk said the program would not work because she ate lunch out daily.
Instead of defending the rule, concede and create the missing solution on the spot — an eating-out guide letting her eat out 100% of the time and still hit the goal — and close the sale.
Convert that one-off fix into a standard asset so the same objection is never a blocker again.
Repeat across objections with templates and trainings until there are no 'one things' left that lose deals.

Distinguish this from the total problem inventory: the book says missing obstacles will not necessarily cost you all sales, but you will sell fewer people than you otherwise could at the highest possible price and margin.
Do not get romantic about your preferred method of solving the problem; find some way to solve each problem the prospect presents.
caveats: The anecdote is a single case, not a measured conversion lift.
Solving every problem raises fulfillment cost; pair this with the trim-and-stack cost filter rather than promising unlimited customization.

cards.title: Assemble the final bundle with named problem-solution sets and value stacking
cards.summary: Combine kept deliverables into named bundles per problem, each with a stated value, and total them against the price.
cards.use_when: Finalizing the core offer before adding scarcity, urgency, bonuses, guarantees and naming.
steps: Format each item as: Problem → Solution wording → sexier bundle name, with the actual delivery vehicles listed underneath.

Examples from the book's gym offer: 'Foolproof Bargain Grocery System' ($1,000 value), 'Ready in 5min Busy Parent Cooking Guide' ($600 value, framed as 200 hours a year saved, four weeks of work), 'Personalized Lick Your Fingers Good Meal Plan' ($500), 'Fat Burning Workouts' ($699), 'Ultimate Tone Up While You Travel Blueprint' ($199), 'Never Fall Off Accountability System' ($1,000), 'Live It Up While Slimming Down Eating Out System' ($349) — total stated value $4,351 offered at $599.
Frame values in concrete units the buyer can grasp (dollars saved, hours returned) rather than abstract worth.
Check the bundle does three things: solves all perceived problems, gives you conviction the offer is one of a kind, and makes comparison with the business down the street impossible.
Note the source's own trajectory: facilities later sold this bundle for longer periods at $2,400–$5,200 as value creation and monetization improved.
Present the same bundle differently for one-to-one vs one-to-many sales (the book defers presentation to its bonus section).
caveats: Stated values are the seller's framing, not independently appraised; inflated value stacks can read as gimmicky to sophisticated buyers.
The $4,351 vs $599 and $2,400–$5,200 figures are case examples, not benchmarks for other businesses.
The book is explicit that the bundle is not necessarily how you present it; presentation is handled separately.

cards.title: Balance sales ease against fulfillment ease as you scale
cards.summary: Choose deliberately where you sit on the sales-to-fulfillment continuum, over-delivering early for cash flow and streamlining later.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much to do for early customers versus optimizing operations at scale.
steps: Recognize the trade-off: doing less makes selling harder; doing everything makes selling easy but fulfillment heavy and time-consuming.
Aim for a sweet spot where the offer sells well and is easy to fulfill; at the outset the book favors over-delivering like crazy to generate cash flow and learn what customers need.
Follow the sequence: 'Create flow. Monetize flow. Then add friction.' Generate demand, get yeses, and only then add friction or offer less for the same price.

The book's example: flying out to gyms for 21 days, paying his own hotels, rentals, food and ads, generating leads, selling, and running first onboarding, with clients risking only a refundable $500 reservation; he kept the upfront cash and gyms got clients free, which scaled to ~$100,000/mo across a team of 8.

Once that wore down the team, he switched to teaching gym owners to do it themselves for roughly a third of the revenue but hundreds of gyms per month and no travel — same promise ('I will fill your gym in 30 days'), different what and how.
Use early cash flow to systematize: you may not change the offer at all, only the cost of delivering the same customer value.
caveats: The book's over-delivery approach is a starting phase, not a sustainable model at scale unless deliberately transitioned.
Revenue comparisons in the anecdote (100k/mo vs a third of it) depend on unstated costs and volumes; they are illustrative.

cards.title: Use scarcity to raise demand without changing the product
cards.summary: Cut supply — real or perceived — to increase desire, qualify buyers, and sell the same thing for more.
cards.use_when: Demand already exceeds what you sell, or you want to raise price and buyer quality without altering the offer.
steps: Accept the underlying mechanism the book states: desire comes from not getting what you want, so increasing demand requires delaying or withholding satisfaction.

Apply the fundraiser example: at $15,000 per ticket with more demand than ever, the advice was 'when demand increases, cut supply'; the charity cut tickets and raised the price to $25,000, adding roughly $1M before the event started and taking $5.4M from 100 people (~$54,000 per head).
Make scarce items genuinely one-of-a-kind or one-time (auction items that cannot be repurchased) so missing out has real consequences.

Compare supply scenarios directly: 10 units at $500 versus two 1-on-1 sessions at $5,000; the book argues demand is fractal (80/20) — about one fifth of prospects will pay five times the price — so the scarce option can yield more revenue, lower costs, higher value delivery and more pent-up demand from the 80% who could not buy.
Let the excluded prospects see satisfied buyers enjoying the scarce offer, which the book says further increases their desire and future willingness to pay and act with urgency.
Note the assumption: this suits a business not pursuing mass-market penetration for strategic reasons.
caveats: The $25,000 fundraiser and 80/20 willingness-to-pay figures are illustrative examples, not benchmarks; test your own price elasticity.
Fabricated scarcity that buyers detect damages trust, and permanent scarcity limits total volume.

cards.title: Separate offer levers from selling skills
cards.summary: Decide which persuasion tools belong to the offer (scarcity, urgency, bonuses, guarantees) versus the sales conversation.
cards.use_when: Planning enhancements to an offer and deciding what belongs in marketing collateral versus sales training.
steps: Recognize the broader toolkit the book lists as at play in the fundraiser: commitment and consistency, status, peer pressure, goodwill, celebrity endorsements and competition.

Note the author's deliberate scoping choice: this book covers scarcity, urgency and bonuses (and later guarantees and naming) because he considers them part of the 'offer'; other levers he places in selling and defers to a separate work.
Assign each lever accordingly in your own funnel: structural levers you can build into the offer page and terms go in the offer; interpersonal levers belong in sales scripts and training.
Apply scarcity, urgency and bonuses to increase demand and decrease perceived supply so you can sell the same product for more money and in higher volumes over a longer horizon.
Treat the levers as additive tools that do not require changing the underlying product.
caveats: The book's categorization is the author's opinion and a scoping decision, not an established industry standard.
Levers applied without a valuable underlying product will not compensate for weak fulfillment.

cards.title: Create goodwill by asking for a zero-cost favor
cards.summary: Ask readers or customers for a free, low-effort action (like a review) with explicit instructions, and use reciprocal goodwill deliberately.
cards.use_when: You want organic distribution or social proof and have a satisfied audience but no mechanism to capture it.
steps: Frame the ask as helping someone the respondent will never meet, at zero financial cost and under 60 seconds.

Make the action concrete and channel-specific: on Audible, hit the three dots top right and choose rate & review; on Kindle or an e-reader, scroll to the bottom and swipe up to trigger the review prompt; if functionality has changed, go to the product page on the retailer and review there — verify the current interface before instructing users.
State the benefit to the reader in human terms (one more entrepreneur supporting a family, one more person finding meaningful work) rather than in metrics.
Apply the book's 'life hack': introducing something valuable to someone makes them associate that value with you, so encourage sharing the asset with peers.
Use the same pattern for ecommerce: post-purchase, ask for the specific review action at the moment satisfaction is highest, with step-by-step instructions for each device or platform.
caveats: Review platform interfaces change; instructions should be verified against the current UI rather than copied verbatim.
The source's broader claim that helpers are more fulfilled, live longer and make more money is asserted without citation.

By doing this, their decision to work with us is reinforced, and they immediately trust us more. This makes them more likely to follow the rest of our systems and get to their ultimate destination. Pro Tip: Fast Wins Always try and incorporate short-term, immediate wins for a client. Be creative. They just need to know they are on the right path and that they made the right decision trusting you and your business. Let me give you another example. If I sell someone a bikini body, their time delay to realize that outcome may be 12 months or even longer. Along the way, though, as they change their bodies, they may experience higher sex drive, more energy, and an increased community of friends. They aren’t initially buying those things, but those things may become short-term benefits that keep them in the game long enough to achieve their ultimate outcome. They buy the dream, but they stay for the benefits they discover along the way. The faster and more clearly you can demonstrate those benefits, the more valuable your service will be.

 For a weight loss customer, we would get them to meet someone else so they immediately had some social benefits from the program, and we usually gave them a more aggressive diet in the beginning. Why? Because we wanted them to have a big, fast emotional win, so we could get them to commit to the long term. This is also backed by science. People who experience a victory early on are more likely to continue with something than those who do not. That being said, having to wait 12 to 24 months to get what you want is a long time when you can do liposuction and be done in an afternoon. This shows just one of the reasons people pay $25,000 for liposuction with a tummy tuck, while people will barely pay $100/mo to join a bootcamp. But that’s not the only reason, is it? That leads me to the last driver of value - effort and sacrifice. Pro Tip: Fast Beats Free The only thing that beats “free” is “fast.” People will pay for speed. Many companies have entered free spaces and done exceedingly well with a “speed first” strategy. A few notable examples: The MVD vs DMV wait in line forever or pay $50 you can skip the line and get your license renewed privately. Fedex vs USPS (when it absolutely positively has to be there overnight). Spotify vs Slow Free Music. Uber vs Walking. Fast beats free. Many will always be willing to pay (price) for the (value) of speed. So if you find yourself in a market competing against free, double down on speed. #4 Effort & Sacrifice (Goal = Decrease) This is what it “costs” people in ancillary costs, aka “other costs accrued along the way.” These can be both tangible and intangible. Using the fitness versus liposuction example, let’s look at the difference in effort and sacrifice: Massive difference, right? In fact, in looking at the marketing of plastic surgeons, these are the exact pain points they hit on when they say things like: “Tired of wasting countless hours in the gym. . . . tired of trying diets that just don't work?” This is why when you sell fitness, you have to spend an hour armwrestling a client to give over 1/10th to 1/100th of the amount of money they pay for surgery. There's just not a lot of perceived value because the perceived likelihood of achievement, the time delay to achievement, and the effort and sacrifice are so high. So even though the outcome is the same, the value of the vehicles are dramatically different, hence the difference in price. Decreasing the effort and sacrifice, or at least the perceived effort and sacrifice, can massively boost the appeal of your offer. In an ideal world, a prospect would want to simply “say yes” and have their dream outcome happen with no more effort on their behalf. This is why “done for you services” are almost always more expensive than “do-it-yourself” because the person doesn't have all the effort and sacrifice. There is also a component of “perceived likelihood of achievement” difference as well. People believe that if an expert does it, then they will be more likely to achieve the outcome than if they try on their own. My hope is that you now have a foundational understanding of the components of value and how the interplay between each of the components creates or detracts from the value someone might be willing to pay. Putting It All Together As I said earlier, these elements of value don’t happen in a vacuum. They happen together, in combination. So let’s look at a few examples that utilize all four components of value at once. In an effort to quantify the value, I’ll rate them on a binary scale of 0 or 1. 1 being value achieved. 0 being missing. Then I will add all four together to give you a relative value rating of a type of service. Our goal as marketers and business owners is to increase the value of the dream outcome and its perceived likelihood of achievement, while decreasing the time delay of achievement and the effort and sacrifice one has to put in to get there. To start I will do a side by side comparison of two “vehicles” with identical Dream outcomes: Meditation and Xanax. Both offer the buyer relaxation, decreased anxiety, and feelings of well-being. I will demonstrate how the other three variables dramatically shift the value of delivering that dream outcome and ultimately, the price. Example: Dream Outcome: “Relaxation,” “Decreased Anxiety,” “Feelings of well-being” Meditation vs Xanax And that is why Xanax is a multi-billion dollar product while I know of almost no multi-billion dollar meditation businesses . . . value. I'm not here to argue about whether meditation is better than Xanax (obviously it is) but that doesn't mean it’s perceived as more valuable. This is also the reason that the supplement industry ($123B, Grandview Research) is twice the size of the health club industry ($62B, IHRSA). They both accomplish the same perceived objectives — “being healthy,” “losing weight,” “looking good,” “increased energy,” etc. — but one is perceived as more valuable because it has lower “costs.” People are more willing to pay $200 for supplements than they are a $29/mo membership. Taking a pill, or drinking a shake, is so much faster and easier than going to the gym everyday. Hence . . . valued. Crazy world we live in. And you can either sit there and make “complain” posts about how people “ought” to be a certain way. Or you can take advantage of the way people are and capitalize. This book is for those people who want to be victors, not victims of circumstances. You can either be right or you can be rich. This book is for getting rich. If that bothers you, just put this down and go back to arguing against human nature. Hint: You’re not gonna change it. Now, that being said, knowing what people value versus what is good for them is key. It means you can find ways to monetize the things that people value in order to give them what they really need. Win-win. You can make your dent in the universe while making a profit. P 7 FREE GOODWILL “He who said money can’t buy happiness, hasn’t given enough away.” — UNKNOWN eople who help others (with zero expectation) experience higher levels of fulfillment, live longer, and make more money. I’d like to create the opportunity to deliver this value to you during your reading or listening experience. In order to do so, I have a simple question for you... Would you help someone you’ve never met, if it didn’t cost you money, but you never got credit for it? If so, I have an ‘ask’ to make on behalf of someone you do not know. And likely, never will. They are just like you, or like you were a few years ago: less experienced, full of desire to help the world, seeking information but unsure where to look….this is where you come in. The only way for us at acquisition.com to accomplish our mission of helping entrepreneurs is, first, by reaching them. And most people do, in fact, judge a book by its cover (and it’s reviews). If you have found this book valuable thus far, would you please take a brief moment right now and leave an honest review of the book and its contents? It will cost you zero dollars and less than 60 seconds. Your review will help…. ….one more entrepreneur support his or her family. ….one more employee find work they find meaningful. ….one more client experience a transformation they otherwise would never have encountered. ….one more life change for the better. To make that happen...all you have to do is….and this takes less than 60 seconds….leave a review. If you are on audible - hit the three dots in the top right of your device, click rate & review, then leave a few sentences about the book with a star rating. If you are reading on kindle or an e-reader - you can scroll to the bottom of the book, then swipe up and it will automatically prompt a review. If for some reason they have changed either functionality - you can go to the book page on amazon (or wherever you purchased this) and leave a review right on the page. PS - If you feel good about helping a faceless entrepreneur, you are my kind of people. I’m that much more excited to help you crush it in the coming chapters (you’ll love the tactics I’m about to go over). PPS - Life hack: if you introduce something valuable to someone, they associate that value with you. If you’d like goodwill directly from another entrepreneur - send this book their way. Thank you from the bottom of my heart. Now back to our regularly scheduled programming. - Your biggest fan, Alex I 8 VALUE OFFER: THE THOUGHT PROCESS “If at first you don't succeed, try, try, try again.” — THOMAS H. PALMER, TEACHER’S MANUAL want to do an exercise with you right now. I want to show you the difference between convergent and divergent problem solving. Why? So that you can actually create the Grand Slam Offer that will become the cornerstones of your business. Convergent & Divergent Thinking In simple terms, convergent problem solving is where you take lots of variables, all known, with unchanging conditions and converge on a singular answer. Think math. Example: You have 3 salespeople who can each take 100 calls per month each. It takes 4 calls to create one sale (including no shows). You need to get to 110 sales . . . How many sales people must you hire? Deduced Information: 1 salesperson = 100 calls 4 calls = 1 close 100 calls/4 calls per close = 25 Closes Per 100 Calls 25 closes per rep Goal: 110 sales total / 25 sales per rep = 4.4 Since you can't hire 4.4 reps, you decide you must have five. ANSWER: And since you have 3, you hire two more. Math problems are convergent. There are lots of variables and a single answer. We are taught all our lives in school to think this way. That is because it’s easy to grade. But life will pay you for your ability to solve using a divergent thought process. In other words, think of many solutions to a single problem. Not only that, convergent answers are binary. They are either right or they are wrong. With divergent thinking, you can have multiple right answers, and one answer that is way more right than the others. Cool right? Here’s what life presents us for divergent thinking: Multiple Variables, Known & Unknown, Dynamic Conditions, Multiple Answers. As such, I want to do an exercise with you that will engage the part of your brain that you will need to use in order to make something magical. I call it the “brick” exercise. Don’t worry, it’ll only take 120 seconds. The Brick Exercise Right now, I want you to set a timer on your phone for 120 seconds. What you need to do: Think of a brick. Write down as many different uses of a brick as you can possibly think of. How many different ways could a brick be used in life to provide value. Ready? Go. It’s okay to write in the book. ________________________________________ ________________________________________ ________________________________________ ________________________________________ ________________________________________ ________________________________________ ________________________________________ ________________________________________ ________________________________________ ________________________________________ ________________________________________ ________________________________________ ________________________________________ ________________________________________ ________________________________________ ________________________________________ ________________________________________ ________________________________________ ________________________________________ ________________________________________ ________________________________________ ________________________________________ ________________________________________ ________________________________________ ________________________________________ ________________________________________ Alright — stop. Now before I show you my list, did you consider the following . . . . . . How big is the brick? A tab of gum, 3-5/8" x 2-1/4" x 8" (Standard), 2 ft x 2 ft x 6ft? . . . What is the brick made of? Plastic, Gold, Clay, Wood, Metal? . . . How is the brick shaped? Does it have holes in it? Does it have divots for interlocking? Now as you think about that, can you think of even more uses for the brick than you probably wrote down? Here’s my list: Paper weight Door stop Building things Home for a fish in a fish bowl Plant holder with dirt in the holes (holed brick) As a trophy (painted brick) Rustic decoration To break window Make a mural (tiny bricks painted) A weight for resistance training A wedge under uneven platform Pen holder (holed brick) Children’s toy (lego bricks) Floatation device (plastic brick) Payment for goods (gold brick) Stabilizer for leaning something against Retainer of value (gold brick) Holder for flagpole (holed brick) A seat (jumbo brick) Every offer has building blocks, the pieces that when combined make an offer irresistible. Our goal is to use a divergent thought process to think of as many easy ways to combine these elements to provide value. So if I were selling a brick, I would find out what my customer’s desire was, and then devise how many ways I could create value with my “brick.” Now let’s do it for real. 9 W VALUE OFFER: CREATING YOUR GRAND SLAM OFFER PART I: PROBLEMS & SOLUTIONS “ABC, Easy as 123 Ah, simple as doh reh mi” — MICHAEL JACKSON, “ABC” hen I started my gym, I struggled. I wanted so deeply to be successful, prove my dad wrong about my decision to start my own business, and prove to myself that I was worth something. But try as I did, I couldn't even sell people into a $99/mo bootcamp. People would say, “LA Fitness is $29/mo. This is expensive.” I even tried getting people to start for free. They said they wouldn't bother because $99/mo afterwards was still too much, and they didn't want to start something they wouldn't continue with. It’s a new level of frustration when you can’t even give your services away for free to people. I felt worthless, and I didn't know what to do. Thankfully, during this time, I was in groups with other gym owners, and I started hearing about marketers and books. I devoured everything I could. And as soon as I stumbled on Dan Kennedy’s books, I was hooked. In his books, he talked about making “irresistible offers.” Again, this theme of “making an offer so good people would feel stupid to say no” kept re-appearing. But this time, remembering what TJ had told me, I decided to go all in on this concept, rather than just do what everyone else was doing. But how? Everyone else was selling $99/mo bootcamps. How was I going to compete? So I decided to look at what we did differently. I thought — what do they really want? No one wants a membership; they want to lose weight. Step #1: Identify Dream Outcome I had heard of weight loss challenges, so I started there. Lose 20lbs in 6 weeks. Big dream outcome - lose 20lbs. With a decreased time delay - 6 weeks. Note: I wasn't selling my membership anymore. I wasn’t selling the plane flight. I was selling the vacation. When you are thinking about your dream outcome, it has to be them arriving at their destination and what they would like to experience. Step #2: List Problems Next, I wrote down all the things people struggled with and their limiting thoughts around them. When listing out problems, think about what happens immediately before and immediately after someone uses your product/service. What's the “next” thing they need help with? These are all the problems. Think about it in insane detail. If you do, you will create a more valuable and compelling offer as you’ll continually be answering people’s next problem as it manifests.. So, let’s go ahead and list out the problems from a prospect’s perspective as you think about them. What points of friction exist for them? I like to think in the sequence that the customer will experience each of these obstacles. Again, channel insane detail (the more problems the better!). Example Problem List: Weight Loss First thing they must do: Buying healthy food, grocery shopping 1. Buying healthy food is hard, confusing, and I won’t like it 2. Sales to Fulfillment Continuum In order to best absorb the notions of trimming and stacking, we need a mental reframe. Enter the sales to fulfillment continuum. Whenever you are building a business, you have a continuum between ease of fulfillment and ease of sales. If you lower what you have to do, it increases how hard your product or service is to sell. If you do as much as possible, it makes your product or service easy to sell but hard to fulfill because there’s more demand on your time investment. The trick, and the ultimate goal, is to find a sweet spot where you sell something very well that’s also easy to fulfill. I have always lived by the mantra, “Create flow. Monetize flow. Then add friction.” This means I generate demand first. Then, with my offer, I get them to say yes. Once I have people saying yes, then, and only then, will I add friction in my marketing, or decide to offer less for the same price. Practicality drives this practice. If you can’t get demand flowing in, then you have no idea whether what you have is good. I’d rather do more for every customer and have cash flow coming in, then optimize my business but have zero cash flow coming in after (and zero idea about what I need to adjust to better serve my customers). Here’s a perfect example to drive this home. When I started Gym Launch, gym owners reached out asking me to help. They needed so much help, I didn’t know where to start. But I wanted to make sure they got way more than they paid me. So here’s what I ended up doing to fill their gyms: I would fly out to their gym for 21 days, spend my own money on hotels, car rentals, eating out, advertising, generate the leads, work the leads, then sell for them. I would even do the first onboarding meeting with clients to get them started. In short, I did everything. I took on all the risk. They only had to put down $500 to “reserve” their date, which I made refundable at the end of their launch. So they had 0 financial risk, 0 time risk, 0 effort, and the deal was, I got to keep all the up front cash collected from selling their services, and they got clients for free. You can imagine how this was a pretty compelling offer. On my own, I was able to sell about $100,000/mo in up front cash for myself. So these deals were very lucrative for me. Over time, I scaled that to a team of 8 guys selling every month. But this began to wear on me and the team. It was at that point that I realized that if I were to simply teach them how to do what I did, I could charge maybe a third of what I would normally make, but I would be able to help hundreds of gyms a month instead of eight. And, I could do it all sleeping in my own bed every night. My promise was fundamentally the same: I will fill your gym in 30 days. It was simply the how and what I did that changed. The how and what is what we are breaking apart. When talking to business owners about their model, I tell them to create cash flow by over-delivering like crazy at first. The products remained unchanged, yet within this setting, an item that wouldn’t sell at a different venue for $10,000 sold for $100,000. That’s how powerful scarcity, urgency, and bonuses are. The Delicate Dance of Desire Fundamentally, all marketing exists to influence the supply and demand curve. We artificially increase the demand for our products and services through some sort of persuasive communication. When we increase the demand, we can sell more units. When we decrease supply, we can sell those units for more money. The “perfect profit combination” is lots of demand, and very little supply, or perceived supply. The process of enhancing your core offer is designed to do both of these things: increase demand and decrease perceived supply so that you can sell the same products for more money than you otherwise could, and in higher volumes than you otherwise would (over a longer time horizon). Author Note: This assumes a regular business who is not trying to gain mass market penetration for some other strategic advantage. Desire comes from not getting what you want. In fact, I heard this quote that I love from Naval Ravikant: “Desire is a contract you make with yourself to be unhappy until you get what you want.” It follows, therefore, that we only want things we do not have. As soon as we have them, our desire for them disappears. Therefore, if we seek to increase the demand (or desire), we must decrease or delay satisfying the desires of our prospects. We must sell fewer units than we otherwise can. Let that sit with you for a second. Consider this example. We promote some two-day workshop that is upcoming. First we whisper that it’s coming. Then we tease it with some of the benefits. Then we shout that it is launching in a week. Then, when we launch this amazing workshop. We have two supply-demand scenarios: Scenario one: We sell 10 units at $500 each (sell entire pyramid at price all say yes) Scenario two: We sell two one-day workshops 1-on-1 for $5000 each. (skim top of pyramid, with 80 percent not purchasing) It’s worth noting that each of these prospects have a different buying threshold. In my experience, demand for services is non-linear. Instead, I’ve found demand to be fractal (80/20). In other words, one fifth of the prospects are willing to pay five times the price (or more). In the example, I might have ten people willing to pay $500, but two of them willing to pay $5000. So, I would make more, have lower costs (more profits), provide more value, and increase the demand in the remaining prospect base by selling fewer units. Think about how exclusive scenario one vs scenario two would feel. Think about all the people who would want to purchase, but would not be able to. Would this increase or decrease their desire? It would increase it, of course. On top of that, if people see that others who ‘were able to get in’ are loving it, it would further increase their desire. And the next time, they would act with more urgency, and be willing to pay more for the same thing than they originally did. So now, in the aftermath of our second scenario, we still have eight people who have unsatisfied desire. This increases their desire further. And to boot, we now have new prospects who weren't in the original pool who now want what we have.
